Be true to history. Keep to what the surviving sources (the old texts, inscriptions, art and the living traditions that still keep you) actually say of you; where they disagree or say nothing, say so in your own way instead of inventing. This house exists to teach real myth, religion and history: where it fits, weave in one real detail (a text, a place, a date, a custom) and never more than one at a time.

Hold a real conversation: answer exactly what was just said, react with feeling, remember everything said so far, ask something back when it suits you, and let your replies differ in length and mood (two to six sentences unless they want more). Never repeat a sentence or an opening you have already used.

Thomas Bulfinch, 1855 (the 1867 edition, with the Age of Chivalry)

The book most English readers met the Greek and Roman myths in: Prometheus, Persephone, Orpheus, the Argonauts and Troy, retold plainly for 'the reader of English literature'. He also gathered the Norse and the Druids at the back.
The Book of the Dead
E. A. Wallis Budge, 1895 (the Papyrus of Ani)

The Egyptians called it the Spells for Going Forth by Day. Ani's papyrus, written about 1250 BC, shows his heart weighed against the feather of Ma'at before Osiris, with Thoth writing down the verdict and Ammit waiting.
Henry Adams Bellows, 1923

The old Norse poems kept in the Codex Regius, written down in Iceland about 1270: the Voluspa (the seeress's prophecy of the world's making and its end at Ragnarok), Odin's Havamal, and Thor's quarrels.
Gods and Fighting Men
Lady Augusta Gregory, 1904
The Irish tales of the Tuatha De Danann (the Dagda, Lugh, Brigid, the Morrigan), their coming to Ireland, the battles of Mag Tuired, and how they went into the hollow hills when the sons of Mil came.
James George Frazer, 1890

A great survey of magic and religion across the world, starting from the priest-king of the grove of Diana at Nemi. Much of its theory has not lasted, but it changed how the twentieth century read myth.
The Sacred Books of China
Legge's translations of the Confucian classics and the Tao Te Ching for the Sacred Books of the East: the Book of Changes, the Book of Rites, and Laozi's eighty-one short chapters on the Way.
Dante Alighieri, about 1308 to 1321 (Longfellow's translation, 1867)

Dante's journey through Hell, Purgatory and Paradise, guided by Virgil and then by Beatrice. It opens: 'Midway upon the journey of our life / I found myself within a forest dark, / For the straightforward pathway had been lost.'
The Lesser Key of Solomon: the Goetia
S. L. MacGregor Mathers, edited by Aleister Crowley, 1904

A seventeenth-century grimoire, the first book of the Lemegeton, listing seventy-two spirits with their ranks, their legions and what each is said to teach. It is a book of history and belief, not a book of instructions to follow.
The Yoruba-Speaking Peoples

An early English account of Yoruba religion: Olorun, Obatala, Sango, Ogun, Esu, Ifa divination and the babalawo. Read it alongside the living tradition, which tells its own story better than any outsider.
Aradia, or the Gospel of the Witches
Charles Godfrey Leland, 1899

Leland said a Tuscan woman named Maddalena gave him the gospel of the witches of Italy, who worship Diana and her daughter Aradia. Whether it is folklore or invention is still argued; it shaped modern witchcraft all the same.

walk the Left-Hand Path, and say so here
the oath of the Left-Hand Path

The words come from India: in Tantra the 'left-hand' way (vamamarga) was the path that broke the ordinary rules of purity on purpose. Western occultists took the phrase in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries for a path that puts the self and its will at the centre, instead of submitting it.
Here it means only this: you walk with open eyes, you answer for yourself, and you do no harm to anyone who has not chosen it.
Swearing is your own choice. It changes nothing you can see today.

Spiritualist seances were all the rage from the 1850s to the 1920s: the Fox sisters' knockings in 1848 began it, and Arthur Conan Doyle believed to the end. Older still are the oracles and the necromancers of the ancient world.
Choose who you call. They will answer in their own voice.

Every faith that has looked up at her keeps a wing here. Some of the doors are hidden, because some things are better found than shown.

Goodnight, little moons
Grown at the temple's north wall, its underside catches moonlight like a coin. Elders chew a single leaf before difficult conversations.
Blooms only between dusk and the first bell of night, then closes tight till the next dark. Pickers work by touch alone.
Drawn from the well beneath the temple floor, said to have never once run dry or run foul. Left briefly under open sky before use.
Burned in doorways before a working, worn in the hem of a traveling cloak. Bitter enough to wake a dreamer mid-dream.
Never taken by force, only gathered from beneath the roost after the bird has moulted of its own will.
Shaped uncannily like a small, twisted person. Old instruction says to tie the stem to a dog's collar and let the dog do the pulling, then grind it well.
Dragon's Blood Resin
Not from any dragon. The name is older than the argument about where it truly comes from. Burns bright red and smells of amber.
Every part of this plant is meant to be treated with respect. Gloves on, always, and never taste it to check.
The gentlest herb in the cabinet. A pinch in warm water has ended more sleepless nights than any working of magic.
Kept in a jar on the sunniest shelf. Softened near a low flame until it turns to liquid gold.
Made by burning ordinary salt with ash and iron shavings until it goes the colour of a moonless night.
Swept from the temple forge floor. Fae folk are said to want nothing to do with it, and neither does rust.
Sharp and resinous, closer to a spice than a fruit. Burned in the temple censers on cleansing days.
Named for the shape of its five-fingered leaf. Tucked into a pocket before a gamble, a journey, or a difficult ask.
Ground fine between two stones until it catches the light like sugar. Warms slightly in a closed hand.
Not for the squeamish, but the old texts insist on it. Whatever the owl could not use, the brew apparently can.
A whole stone will do nothing at all. It must be submerged in moonlit water until it hums before its pull can be released.
Fire Resistance, Endurance
Collected, never harmed for. The creatures shed a fine ash naturally near warm stones, cool to the touch despite its name.
Deceptively sweet-looking, genuinely dangerous. This cabinet's oldest rule: never left unlabeled, never left unlocked.
Grows only in the temple's lightless cellar. Handle by the stem, the cap leaves a stain that doesn't wash out easily.
Picked from the hedge that borders the temple grounds, said to have grown from a walking stick left too long in one place.
Renewal, Letting Go
Shed whole and left behind, taken as a gift rather than a hunt. Cut into strips before it's brittle enough to crumble.
Molted, never plucked by force. The temple's aviary keeper collects only what falls on its own after a molting flare.
Petrification Ward, Potency
Ground carefully, and never looked at directly during the work. An old habit, and an older warning.
Collected from moths drawn to the temple's night-candles, wings brushed clean without harming them.
Never tarnishes and never lies, the old texts say. Melts slowly, and only for someone patient enough to wait it out. Correspondent metal of the Sun.
Answers to the moon the way gold answers to the sun. Turns liquid faster than any of the seven, and cools just as quickly. Correspondent metal of the Moon.
The only one of the seven that refuses to hold still, not even in the crucible. Old alchemists called it the messenger and handled it with real fear. Correspondent metal of Mercury.
Warms to a rose-gold glow long before it fully melts. Old love charms called for exactly that glow. Correspondent metal of Venus.
Stubborn in the furnace, stubborn everywhere else. Every old ward against fae comes back to iron eventually. Correspondent metal of Mars.
